strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: synthetic pre-training for time series classification addresses severe data scarcity, curation overhead, and out-of-distribution evaluation contamination in existing real-world archives.

Principled pipeline design: combining Gaussian Process kernel compositions (with explicit mean functions) and Structural Causal Models (SCMs) provides a sound mechanism to inject both temporal patterns (trends, seasonality) and nonlinear multi-component cluster structures.

First comprehensive investigation of scaling laws in time series classification foundation models, demonstrating clear, monotonic scaling across data size (10K to 10M), model capacity (up to 783M parameters), and training epochs, in contrast to the noisy or saturated behavior observed with real benchmarks (e.g., UEA).

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: experiments cover 128 UCR datasets, 17 WOODS out-of-distribution datasets, irregular multivariate clinical datasets (P12, P19), fine-tuning regimes, and cross-task transfer to zero-shot forecasting with Chronos.

Thorough representation and qualitative analyses, including ablation studies (Table 1), run-time breakdown (Table 2), CKA similarity and linearity diagnostics (Figure 5), UMAP parameter alignment, attention rollout maps, and Sliced Wasserstein Distance comparisons.
weaknesses: Conceptual gap between causal graph propagation and univariate training: since pre-training treats each node's trajectory as an independent univariate sample, the paper could provide more theoretical or empirical intuition explaining why multivariate DAG propagation benefits univariate marginal representations beyond acting as random nonlinear feature transforms.
Absence of neural generative baselines (e.g., diffusion- or GAN-based time series generators), although procedural generation is much faster and more scalable.

Minor layout and visual clarity issues: subplots in Figure 3 are quite compact and hard to read, and there are minor label/caption inconsistencies (e.g., referencing 'CauK' instead of 'CauKer' in Figure 3 caption).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and significant problem in time series representation learning: pre-training time series foundation models (TSFMs) using purely synthetic data, thereby circumventing data scarcity, licensing/privacy constraints, and test-set contamination issues.

The proposed CAUKER framework is conceptually well-motivated and elegant, successfully bridging Gaussian Process kernel compositions (for local/global temporal dynamics such as periodicity, trends, and non-stationarity) with Structural Causal Models (for non-linear dependencies and cluster structures).

The empirical investigation into scaling laws is thorough and insightful. The authors demonstrate that while scaling on real-world datasets (e.g., UEA) suffers from saturation and irregular behavior due to domain heterogeneity and imbalance, pre-training on CAUKER exhibits consistent and predictable scaling in terms of dataset size, model capacity (from 0.75M to 783M parameters), and optimization epochs.

The evaluation is comprehensive across multiple dimensions: it tests two distinct foundation model architectures and objectives (Mantis with contrastive ViT and MOMENT with masked reconstruction T5), includes diverse benchmarks (UCR, WOODS, irregular clinical data P12/P19), ablations of components and hyperparameters, and an intriguing extension showing competitive zero-shot forecasting on Chronos.
weaknesses: The connection between the SCM data generation process and downstream classification performance could be more formally characterized. Since pre-training is strictly self-supervised (contrastive or masked autoencoding on individual univariate series) without explicit class labels, the mechanism by which SCM propagation creates discriminative feature clusters could be analyzed more deeply beyond empirical DTW distance matrices and UMAP plots.

There are minor formatting and referencing inconsistencies in the presentation. For instance, on Page 9 and 10, the text refers to Table 7 for pre-training performance comparisons, but the corresponding floating environment on Page 10 is labeled as 'Figure 7' (which embeds both a table and loss plots), while another Table 7 appears in Appendix E for the scaling law accuracy numbers.

The baseline choice for real-world pre-training in the scaling experiments relies exclusively on slicing UEA (30 datasets flattened into univariate series). While the authors explain this choice, UEA comprises relatively few distinct domains with severe class imbalances, which naturally predisposes it to poor scaling behavior compared to a smoothly parameterized synthetic generator.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored gap in time series foundation models (TSFMs): while synthetic pre-training has achieved notable success in forecasting and tabular learning, classification-oriented foundation models have largely relied on curated real-world corpora.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering two distinct self-supervised paradigms and architectures (contrastive ViT-based Mantis and masked autoencoding T5-based MOMENT) across 128 UCR datasets, 17 WOODS OOD datasets, irregular multivariate clinical benchmarks (P12, P19), and zero-shot forecasting.

Rigorous investigation of data and model scaling laws, providing clear empirical evidence that synthetic data allows monotonic scaling across model sizes (up to 783M parameters) and dataset sizes (up to 10M samples), whereas real-world UEA data exhibits saturation and instability.

Extensive analysis of learned representations and generator behavior, including wall-clock time breakdown, hyperparameter sensitivity on DAG structure, Sliced Wasserstein distance, CKA layer similarity, and attention rollout visualizations.
weaknesses: Conceptual and algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: CAUKER largely marries the composite Gaussian Process kernel sampling from KernelSynth/Chronos with the feed-forward DAG propagation from TabPFN, without introducing fundamentally new generative modeling principles.

The 'causal' framing is somewhat overstated: the pipeline constructs a random directed acyclic graph (DAG) of nonlinear transformations to propagate continuous processes. There is no causal identification, interventional validation, or causal inference involved; it is essentially a random feedforward computational graph.

There is a conceptual gap between the classification motivation and the self-supervised training setup: the paper motivates the SCM via cluster separability, yet the models are trained using purely unsupervised objectives (patch reconstruction for MOMENT, instance-level augmentations for Mantis) without synthetic class labels. More theoretical or empirical justification for why the DAG propagation specifically aids instance contrastive / masked pretraining beyond acting as a nonlinear mixing function would strengthen the work.

Minor presentation and referencing inconsistencies in the main text (e.g., on page 9, the text references 'Table 7' to discuss the pre-training comparison, but the corresponding artifact on page 10 is labeled 'Figure 7', while Table 7 in Appendix E is an accuracy table for scaling laws).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: while synthetic pretraining has shown strong potential in tabular data (TabPFN) and time series forecasting (Chronos, ForecastPFN, TimePFN), this is one of the first works to systematically develop and study synthetic data pretraining specifically tailored for time series classification foundation models.

The CAUKER methodology is well-motivated and conceptually sound: combining Gaussian Process kernel composition (with non-zero mean functions) with Structural Causal Model (SCM) propagation over directed acyclic graphs injects both realistic temporal dynamics and non-linear structured dependencies.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two distinct pretraining paradigms: contrastive learning (Mantis, ViT-based) and masked autoencoding (MOMENT, T5-based), evaluated across the full 128-dataset UCR benchmark.

Thorough investigation of scaling behavior: the paper provides empirical scaling analyses across dataset scale (10K to 10M samples), model size (up to 783M parameters), and optimization horizon, showing that CAUKER exhibits significantly smoother scaling trends than real-world pretraining subsets (UEA).
Insightful qualitative and representational analyses, including Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), activation non-linearity metrics, and parameter-disentanglement visualizations via UMAP.
weaknesses: Presentation and referencing issues in the manuscript: on page 9, the text refers to 'Table 6', but the corresponding element on page 10 is presented as a hybrid table/figure labeled 'Figure 6'. In addition, Footnote 2 on page 15 is empty, and the subplots in Figure 3 are small and cramped with overlapping legend references in the caption.

Ablation of graph/SCM topology is somewhat limited: while Table 1 clearly shows CAUKER outperforming Mean+KernelSynth, the paper lacks detailed ablations investigating the role of DAG properties (e.g., graph density, node depth, number of parents) on representation quality for downstream classification.

Evaluation scope is primarily focused on the UCR univariate benchmark: given that real-world time series classification often involves multivariate series, expanding the downstream zero-shot evaluation to multivariate datasets (e.g., UEA archive, physiological benchmarks) would significantly bolster the generality of the conclusions.

The baseline choice for real-world pretraining (UEA split into univariate channels) introduces potential domain bias and channel-correlation loss, which might partly explain why UEA scales poorly compared to CAUKER.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge: while synthetic pretraining has shown strong success in time series forecasting (e.g., Chronos, ForecastPFN) and tabular data (TabPFN), classification-tailored synthetic pretraining for time series foundation models (TSFMs) has remained largely unexplored.

The proposed CAUKER framework intuitively bridges Gaussian Process kernel composition (capturing local temporal smoothness, trends, and periodicity) with Structural Causal Models (introducing realistic non-linear transformations and cluster-like structures advantageous for classification).

Comprehensive empirical investigation: evaluated on 128 UCR benchmark datasets across two distinct pretraining paradigms and architectures—contrastive ViT-based Mantis and masked reconstruction T5-based MOMENT.

Extensive analysis of neural scaling laws (dataset size scaling from 10K to 10M, model parameter scaling up to 783M, and training time scaling), supported by qualitative and representational analyses (CKA, non-linearity metrics, and UMAP projections).
weaknesses: Missing formal pseudocode: Section 3.2 and Section 4 refer to complete pseudocode in Appendix C, but Appendix C.1 contains only a brief textual summary rather than an explicit algorithmic box or pseudocode listing exact DAG sampling parameters (e.g., graph density, node count distributions).
Referencing inconsistencies: Section 4.5 refers to results presented in 'Table 6', which appears to actually be the table inside Figure 6 on page 10.

Unclear mechanistic role of the DAG for univariate pretraining: Because the downstream models are trained and evaluated on univariate series (treating graph nodes individually), the causal DAG effectively serves as a composition of non-linear transformations over mixed GP priors. Additional ablation isolating the DAG topology versus random non-linear feedforward mixtures would clarify the exact role played by causal graph propagation.

Evaluation is restricted to univariate zero-shot classification; given that SCMs naturally yield multi-variable systems, testing multivariate benchmarks (such as UEA classification) in a native multivariate setup would substantially strengthen the empirical scope.

strengths: Relevant and timely problem: Pretraining Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) purely on synthetic data is a compelling direction to address data scarcity, curation overhead, and data leakage in time series classification.

Dual-paradigm evaluation: The paper systematically benchmarks the proposed synthetic data generation pipeline across two fundamentally different self-supervised learning paradigms: contrastive learning (Mantis) and masked autoencoding (MOMENT).
Comprehensive experimental scope on UCR: The empirical evaluation spans all 128 datasets in the UCR benchmark, covering a wide array of time series lengths, domains, and class numbers.

Insightful representation diagnostics: The inclusion of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) and layer-wise non-linearity analyses provides interesting qualitative evidence on how synthetic versus real data affects representation learning across model depth.
weaknesses: Flawed baseline for real-world scaling comparison: The central claim that 'scaling laws are broken when using common classification benchmarks' relies entirely on slicing subsets of the UEA benchmark. The UEA benchmark consists of only 30 multivariate datasets, sliced channel-wise into univariate series. Because the number of distinct source distributions is extremely small (30), scaling up sample counts within UEA primarily increases repetition rather than semantic diversity. Comparing this to unbounded, diverse synthetic data makes the conclusion about real-world scaling unfair and overclaimed.

Marginal improvement over simpler synthetic baselines: In Table 1, CAUKER achieves 78.31% on Mantis, whereas the simpler Mean-KernelSynth baseline achieves 78.20% (a mere 0.11% difference). Given that CAUKER introduces significant algorithmic complexity (DAG sampling, activation banks, and linear mixing), the marginal gain over standard GP sampling with non-zero mean functions weakens the case for the causal graph component.

Technical novelty is largely combinatorial: The generation method directly concatenates Gaussian Process kernel composition from Chronos (Ansari et al., 2024) with the SCM DAG propagation structure from TabPFN (Hollmann et al., 2023), without significant theoretical or methodological adaptations specifically designed for time series classification.

Restricted to univariate classification: While the SCM propagation in Step 5 naturally generates multivariate coupled systems, all generated data and evaluations are restricted to univariate sequences (length 512). Not evaluating multivariate classification on UEA leaves the primary strength of causal multi-node graphs unverified.

Presentation and referencing defects: Several editorial and formatting issues are present throughout the draft. In Section 4.5, the text references 'Table 6', but the corresponding results are embedded inside a combined figure/table labeled 'Figure 6' on page 10. Appendix C.1 promises 'complete pseudocode of this procedure', but no algorithm box is included. Additionally, Footnote 2 on page 15 is left empty.
